chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Safwan ibn Yahya and Fadalah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two of them عليهما السلام, who said:

I said: If a man closes the eyes of the dead person, is ghusl (ritual bath) required upon him? He said: “If he touches him while his warmth remains, then no; but if he touches him after he has become cold, then let him perform ghusl (ritual bath).”
I said: Then the one who washes him performs ghusl (ritual bath)? He said: “Yes.”

I said: So he washes him, then clothes him in his shrouds before performing ghusl (ritual bath)? He said: “He washes him, then washes his hands up to the shoulders, then clothes him in his shrouds, then performs ghusl (ritual bath).”
I said: Then the one who carries him, is ghusl (ritual bath) required upon him? He said: “No.”
I said: Then the one who places him into the grave, is wudu (ablution) required upon him? He said: “No, unless he wishes to perform wudu (ablution) because of the dust of the grave.”

key_terms.بِحَرَارَتِهِ: while the body's warmth still remains
key_terms.تُرَابِ: dust or soil, here referring to the grave's earth
key_terms.غُسْلٌ: ritual bath required in certain cases related to the deceased

ai.seo_question: When is ghusl (ritual bath) required after touching or washing a dead body in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith explains the rulings related to touching and washing the deceased. It states that touching the dead body after it has cooled requires ghusl (ritual bath), that the washer of the deceased performs ghusl, and that merely carrying or placing the deceased into the grave does not itself require ghusl or wudu (ablution), except optionally due to grave dust.
